newsitem.title: LEBANON: Red Army case in Lebanon leaves trail of mystery.
newsitem.headline: Red Army case in Lebanon leaves trail of mystery.

text.p: It has many of the ingredients of an international thriller: wanted Red Army guerrillas, double agents and political intrigue from the Middle East to Japan.
And it has left a trail of unanswered questions leading from Beirut to Tokyo, Damascus and maybe to Washington.
The confusing case of the Japanese Red Army guerrillas arrested in Lebanon last month publicly humiliated Tokyo just when it was about to help Lebanon's reconstruction.
It probably also hurt Syrian ties with Tokyo and perhaps also with Washington, Beirut analysts say.

Why did Lebanese security agents arrest the five ageing guerrillas who had lived in Lebanon for years? And who told Japan so that Tokyo announced the arrests before Beirut and sent a team of agents to help identify the suspects?
And then why did Lebanon dither for three weeks after the arrests, refusing to let the Japanese interrogate the guerrillas, before finally refusing to hand them over?

The five are wanted by Japan on charges arising from Red Army operations dating to the 1970s -- plane hijackings, hostage takings and a 1972 attack on Tel Aviv's Lod airport that killed 24 people and injured 78.
But on Thursday Lebanon charged them with passport and forgery offences that carried long jail terms and ensured they could not be extradited for years.
Beirut newspapers and judicial sources close to the affair said it all began as an accident.

State Security agents stumbled on the guerrillas after arresting an Asian during a passport forgery investigation in Beirut. The government was embarrassed when Japan said they were Red Army and asked for extradition, they said.
At that point Syria, which has 35,000 troops in Lebanon and backs hardline Palestinian groups allied to the Red Army, ordered a halt, the newspapers and judicial sources said.

But if the arrests really were an accident, why had Brigadier Ali Makki, second in command of State Security, recently visited Japan? And why was his resignation accepted once the guerrillas were charged?
"I think Lebanese intelligence was trying to do a deal directly with the Japanese embassy to hand over the guerrillas," said a Western diplomat. "Then the Syrians stepped in."
But Lebanon's State Security agency is formally under the control of Prime Minister Rafik al-Hariri and some Beirut newspapers pointed accusing fingers at him.

Could Hariri have agreed with Washington and Japan to hand over the guerrillas as part of the price for last December's Friends of Lebanon donors conference in Washington that pledged $3.2 billion to Lebanese reconstruction, they asked.

U.S. newspapers certainly speculated gleefully at the time of the arrests that Lebanon was trying to clean up its image by cracking down on wanted international guerrillas, a move sure to please Washington.
But there has been no sign since then of Syrian displeasure with Hariri, indicating he is not suspected of involvement.

The analysts said a key unanswered question related to three other arrested Japanese who were released when the guerrillas were charged. Newspapers speculated that two of them were Japanese double agents who infiltrated the guerrillas.

But one analyst was sure of one thing: "I think Beirut's relations with Japan may suffer from this. The Japanese have taken a slap and they have gone home with empty hands. I should not be surprised if they respond to Lebanon and Syria.
"We will have to watch Japanese investments," he said.
